claim: Atg9 encodes a multipass transmembrane protein thought to act as a membrane carrier for forming autophagosomes.
source: Autophagy-related gene 9 (Atg9) encodes a multipass transmembrane protein thought to act as a membrane carrier for forming autophagosomes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as established knowledge about Atg9 function.

claim: Loss of Atg9 led to shortened lifespan in Drosophila.
source: Here, we generated Atg9 null mutant flies and found that loss of Atg9 led to shortened lifespan, locomotor defects, and increased susceptibility to stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Atg9 null mutant flies shown in the manuscript.

claim: Loss of Atg9 led to locomotor defects in Drosophila.
source: Here, we generated Atg9 null mutant flies and found that loss of Atg9 led to shortened lifespan, locomotor defects, and increased susceptibility to stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Atg9 null mutant flies shown in the manuscript.

claim: Loss of Atg9 led to increased susceptibility to stress in Drosophila.
source: Here, we generated Atg9 null mutant flies and found that loss of Atg9 led to shortened lifespan, locomotor defects, and increased susceptibility to stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Atg9 null mutant flies shown in the manuscript.

claim: Atg9 loss resulted in aberrant adult midgut morphology with dramatically enlarged enterocytes.
source: Atg9 loss also resulted in aberrant adult midgut morphology with dramatically enlarged enterocytes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental observations and imaging data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Inhibiting the TOR signaling pathway rescued the midgut defects of the Atg9 mutants.
source: Interestingly, inhibiting the TOR signaling pathway rescued the midgut defects of the Atg9 mutants.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing rescue of phenotypes through TOR inhibition.

claim: Atg9 interacted with PALS1-associated tight junction protein (Patj).
source: In addition, Atg9 interacted with PALS1-associated tight junction protein (Patj), which associates with TSC2 to regulate TOR activity.
evidence: This claim is supported by biochemical interaction data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Patj associates with TSC2 to regulate TOR activity.
source: In addition, Atg9 interacted with PALS1-associated tight junction protein (Patj), which associates with TSC2 to regulate TOR activity.
evidence: This is supported by both data in the manuscript and citation to previous work.

claim: Depletion of Atg9 caused a marked decrease in TSC2 levels.
source: Depletion of Atg9 caused a marked decrease in TSC2 levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot and immunofluorescence data in the manuscript.

claim: Atg9 antagonizes TOR signaling in the regulation of cell growth and tissue homeostasis.
source: Our findings revealed an antagonistic relationship between Atg9 and TOR signaling in the regulation of cell growth and tissue homeostasis.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from multiple experimental observations in the manuscript.

claim: Autophagy is essential for maintaining cellular homeostasis and survival under various stress conditions.
source: Autophagy is essential for maintaining cellular homeostasis and survival under various stress conditions.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field.

claim: There is increasing evidence of the importance of autophagy in differentiation, development, aging, and tumorigenesis.
source: There is increasing evidence of the importance of autophagy in a variety of physiological and pathological processes, including differentiation, development, aging, and tumorigenesis (Jiang and Mizushima, 2014; Mizushima and Levine, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The autophagic pathway is controlled by a series of evolutionarily conserved autophagy-related (Atg) proteins to generate double-membraned vesicles, the autophagosomes.
source: The autophagic pathway is controlled by a series of evolutionarily conserved autophagy-related (Atg) proteins to generate double-membraned vesicles, the autophagosomes, which subsequently fuse with lysosomes for the degradation of their contents (Feng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field supported by citation.

claim: Autophagosomes subsequently fuse with lysosomes for the degradation of their contents.
source: The autophagic pathway is controlled by a series of evolutionarily conserved autophagy-related (Atg) proteins to generate double-membraned vesicles, the autophagosomes, which subsequently fuse with lysosomes for the degradation of their contents (Feng et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field supported by citation.

claim: Atg9 is the only multi-spanning transmembrane protein in the Atg family.
source: Atg9 is the only multi-spanning transmembrane protein in the family and is involved in promoting lipid transport to autophagosomes during their formation (Tooze, 2010; Yamamoto et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Atg9 is involved in promoting lipid transport to autophagosomes during their formation.
source: Atg9 is the only multi-spanning transmembrane protein in the family and is involved in promoting lipid transport to autophagosomes during their formation (Tooze, 2010; Yamamoto et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In yeast, Atg9 cycles between cytoplasmic membrane pools and the preautophagosomal structure (PAS).
source: In yeast, distinct from other Atg proteins, Atg9 cycles between cytoplasmic membrane pools and the preautophagosomal structure (PAS) (Mari et al., 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge from yeast studies supported by citation.

claim: The Atg9-containing vesicles are recruited to PAS by the Atg1-kinase complex during autophagosome formation.
source: The Atg9-containing vesicles are recruited to PAS by the Atg1-kinase complex during autophagosome formation (Rao et al., 2016; Suzuki et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Mammalian Atg9 (mAtg9) localizes to the trans-Golgi network, endosomal system, and plasma membrane under normal conditions.
source: Similarly, mammalian Atg9 (mAtg9) localizes to the trans-Golgi network, endosomal system, and plasma membrane under normal conditions, whereas it translocates to autophagic membranes upon autophagy induction (Orsi et al., 2012; Popovic and Dikic, 2014; Puri et al., 2013; Young et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge from mammalian studies supported by citations.

claim: Mammalian Atg9 translocates to autophagic membranes upon autophagy induction.
source: Similarly, mammalian Atg9 (mAtg9) localizes to the trans-Golgi network, endosomal system, and plasma membrane under normal conditions, whereas it translocates to autophagic membranes upon autophagy induction (Orsi et al., 2012; Popovic and Dikic, 2014; Puri et al., 2013; Young et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge from mammalian studies supported by citations.

claim: The trafficking of mAtg9 is important for autophagy induction.
source: The trafficking of mAtg9 is important for autophagy induction, and several proteins, including Ulk1, ZIPK, p38IP, TRAPPC8, TBC1D5, and the AP2 complex (Imai et al., 2016; Lamb et al., 2016; Popovic and Dikic, 2014; Tang et al., 2011; Webber and Tooze, 2010; Young et al., 2006), regulate the spatio‐temporal distribution of mAtg9 during autophagy.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Several proteins including Ulk1, ZIPK, p38IP, TRAPPC8, TBC1D5, and the AP2 complex regulate the spatio-temporal distribution of mAtg9 during autophagy.
source: The trafficking of mAtg9 is important for autophagy induction, and several proteins, including Ulk1, ZIPK, p38IP, TRAPPC8, TBC1D5, and the AP2 complex (Imai et al., 2016; Lamb et al., 2016; Popovic and Dikic, 2014; Tang et al., 2011; Webber and Tooze, 2010; Young et al., 2006), regulate the spatio‐temporal distribution of mAtg9 during autophagy.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: mAtg9 can modulate dsDNA-induced innate immune responses by regulating the STING-TBK1 assembly.
source: In addition to autophagy, mAtg9 can modulate dsDNA-induced innate immune responses by regulating the STING-TBK1assembly (Saitoh et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: mAtg9 plays a role in necrotic programmed cell death during bone morphogenesis.
source: Recently, Imagawa et al showed that mAtg9 also plays a role in necrotic programmed cell death during bone morphogenesis (Imagawa et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Drosophila Atg9 functions as an essential component of autophagy.
source: Our previous study in Drosophila showed that Atg9 functions not only as an essential component of autophagy, but also interacts with Drosophila tumor necrosis factor receptor-associated factor 2 (dTRAF2) to regulate ROS-induced c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) signaling, including JNK-mediated autophagy activation and intestinal stem cell (ISC) proliferation (Tang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by previous work from the authors' lab, cited in the text.

claim: Drosophila Atg9 interacts with dTRAF2 to regulate ROS-induced JNK signaling.
source: Our previous study in Drosophila showed that Atg9 functions not only as an essential component of autophagy, but also interacts with Drosophila tumor necrosis factor receptor-associated factor 2 (dTRAF2) to regulate ROS-induced c-Jun N-terminal kinase (JNK) signaling, including JNK-mediated autophagy activation and intestinal stem cell (ISC) proliferation (Tang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by previous work from the authors' lab, cited in the text.

claim: Oxidative stress-induced autophagy can inhibit JNK activity through a negative feedback mechanism.
source: Moreover, oxidative stress-induced autophagy can inhibit JNK activity through a negative feedback mechanism to prevent the over-activation of JNK-mediated stress responses, thereby helping the maintenance of midgut homeostasis.
evidence: This is based on previous work from the authors' lab.

claim: TOR functions as a central player in the regulation of cell growth and metabolism in response to various environmental stimuli.
source: Target of rapamycin (TOR), a serine/threonine kinase, functions as a central player in the regulation of cell growth and metabolism in response to various environmental stimuli, including nutrient status, growth factors, and amino acids (Saxton and Sabatini, 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Under nutrient-rich conditions, TOR promotes protein synthesis and energy metabolism while suppressing autophagy.
source: Under nutrient-rich conditions, TOR promotes protein synthesis and energy metabolism while suppressing autophagy (Russell et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Under nutrient deprivation conditions, TOR is inhibited, leading to the induction of autophagy.
source: Under nutrient deprivation conditions, TOR is inhibited, leading to the induction of autophagy.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: TOR negatively regulates autophagy by phosphorylating and inhibiting Atg1/Ulk1 complex activity.
source: TOR negatively regulates autophagy by phosphorylating and inhibiting Atg1/Unc51-like kinase 1 (Ulk1) complex activity (Alers et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The Atg1/Ulk1 kinase acts as the most upstream autophagy regulator for the initiation of autophagosome formation.
source: The Atg1/Ulk1 kinase is thought to act as the most upstream autophagy regulator for the initiation of autophagosome formation (Itakura and Mizushima, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Atg1/Ulk1 recruits downstream Atg proteins to the phagophore assembly site.
source: Atg1/Ulk1 recruits downstream Atg proteins to the phagophore assembly site and phosphorylates several Atg proteins, including the Ambra1/Beclin1/Vps34 complex and Atg9 (Cheong et al., 2008; Di Bartolomeo et al., 2010; Papinski et al., 2014; Russell et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Atg1/Ulk1 phosphorylates several Atg proteins, including the Ambra1/Beclin1/Vps34 complex and Atg9.
source: Atg1/Ulk1 recruits downstream Atg proteins to the phagophore assembly site and phosphorylates several Atg proteins, including the Ambra1/Beclin1/Vps34 complex and Atg9 (Cheong et al., 2008; Di Bartolomeo et al., 2010; Papinski et al., 2014; Russell et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Atg1/Ulk1 can negatively regulate TOR signaling in Drosophila and mammals.
source: Interestingly, recent studies have shown that Atg1/Ulk1 can negatively regulate TOR signaling in Drosophila and mammals (Lee et al., 2007; Scott et al., 2007), suggesting a tight interplay between Atg1/Ulk1-dependent autophagy and TOR-mediated cell growth.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Loss of Atg9 severely impairs starvation-induced autophagy.
source: Here, we generated null mutants for Drosophila Atg9, and showed that loss of Atg9 severely impairs starvation-induced and developmental autophagy.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Loss of Atg9 severely impairs developmental autophagy.
source: Here, we generated null mutants for Drosophila Atg9, and showed that loss of Atg9 severely impairs starvation-induced and developmental autophagy.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Atg9 null mutant flies exhibited dramatically reduced lifespans.
source: Atg9 null mutant flies exhibited dramatically reduced lifespans, climbing defects, and hypersensitivity to stress.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Atg9 null mutant flies exhibited climbing defects.
source: Atg9 null mutant flies exhibited dramatically reduced lifespans, climbing defects, and hypersensitivity to stress.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Atg9 null mutant flies exhibited hypersensitivity to stress.
source: Atg9 null mutant flies exhibited dramatically reduced lifespans, climbing defects, and hypersensitivity to stress.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Ablation of Atg9 caused increased TOR activity in the adult Drosophila midgut.
source: Surprisingly, ablation of Atg9 also caused increased TOR activity and aberrant enlargement of intestinal epithelial cells in the adult Drosophila midgut.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Ablation of Atg9 caused aberrant enlargement of intestinal epithelial cells in the adult Drosophila midgut.
source: Surprisingly, ablation of Atg9 also caused increased TOR activity and aberrant enlargement of intestinal epithelial cells in the adult Drosophila midgut.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Similar intestinal defects were observed in Atg1, Atg13 and Atg17/Fip200 depletion mutants.
source: Similar intestinal defects were observed in Atg1, Atg13 and Atg17/Fip200 depletion mutants.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: In mammals, the polarity protein Patj interacts with tuberous sclerosis complex 2 (TSC2) to regulate TOR activity.
source: In mammals, the polarity protein Patj interacts with tuberous sclerosis complex 2 (TSC2), a negative regulator of TOR signaling, to regulate TOR activity (Massey-Harroche et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge from mammalian studies supported by citation.

claim: Overexpression of Patj suppressed adult midgut defects of Atg9 mutants.
source: Strikingly, overexpression of Patj and TSC1-TSC2 suppressed adult midgut defects of Atg9 mutants.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Overexpression of TSC1-TSC2 suppressed adult midgut defects of Atg9 mutants.
source: Strikingly, overexpression of Patj and TSC1-TSC2 suppressed adult midgut defects of Atg9 mutants.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: The homozygous Atg9Gal4KO and Atg9d51 flies are semi-lethal, with a few escapers.
source: The homozygous Atg9Gal4KO and Atg9d51 flies and trans-heterozygous Atg9Gal4KO/Atg9d51 flies are semi-lethal, with a few escapers.
evidence: This is an observation from generating the mutant flies.

claim: Trans-heterozygous Atg9Gal4KO/Atg9d51 flies are semi-lethal, with a few escapers.
source: The homozygous Atg9Gal4KO and Atg9d51 flies and trans-heterozygous Atg9Gal4KO/Atg9d51 flies are semi-lethal, with a few escapers.
evidence: This is an observation from generating the mutant flies.

claim: Atg9 mutant escapers produce no offspring, suggesting fertility defects.
source: Interestingly, the escapers produce no offspring, suggesting fertility defects in Atg9 mutants.
evidence: This is an observation from the mutant flies with inference about fertility.

claim: Atg9 expression is absent in Atg9Gal4KO and Atg9d51 mutants.
source: We confirmed the lack of Atg9 expression in the mutants by RT-PCR and Western blot analysis (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR and Western blot data shown in Figure 1B and C.

claim: The gene expression and semi-lethality of Atg9 mutants can be fully rescued by a 5.8 kb genomic construct encompassing the Atg9 transcript and its endogenous regulatory regions.
source: Importantly, the gene expression and semi-lethality of Atg9 mutants can be fully rescued by a 5.8 kb genomic construct encompassing the Atg9 transcript and its endogenous regulatory regions (Figure 1A–C).
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiments shown in Figure 1.

claim: Atg9Gal4KO and Atg9d51 specifically disrupt Atg9 function and act as null mutants.
source: These results demonstrated that Atg9Gal4KO and Atg9d51 specifically disrupt Atg9 function and act as null mutants.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the characterization data of the mutants.

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of Atg9 inhibits starvation-induced autophagy in the larval fat body.
source: RNAi-mediated knockdown of Atg9 inhibits starvation-induced autophagy and developmental autophagy in the larval fat body (Bader et al., 2015; Tang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citations.

claim: RNAi-mediated knockdown of Atg9 inhibits developmental autophagy in the larval fat body.
source: RNAi-mediated knockdown of Atg9 inhibits starvation-induced autophagy and developmental autophagy in the larval fat body (Bader et al., 2015; Tang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge from previous studies supported by citations.

claim: Loss of Atg9 dramatically blocked the starvation-induced punctate LysoTracker Green staining in larval fat body.
source: Notably, loss of Atg9 dramatically blocked the starvation-induced punctate staining, compared to the controls (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by LysoTracker staining data shown in Figure 1D and E.

claim: Inhibiting autophagic activity often results in the accumulation of autophagic substrate p62/SQSTM1 and ubiquitinated protein aggregates.
source: Because inhibiting autophagic activity often results in the accumulation of autophagic substrate p62/SQSTM1 and ubiquitinated protein aggregates (Komatsu and Ichimura, 2010), we investigated the effect of Atg9 on protein ubiquitination and autophagic degradation of Ref(2)P, the Drosophila homolog of p62.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Atg9 mutants had a dramatic increase in Ref(2)p levels.
source: Compared to the control, Atg9 mutants had a dramatic increase in Ref(2)p levels and ubiquitin aggregate formation (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot and immunostaining data shown in Figure 1F and G.

claim: Atg9 mutants had a dramatic increase in ubiquitin aggregate formation.
source: Compared to the control, Atg9 mutants had a dramatic increase in Ref(2)p levels and ubiquitin aggregate formation (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot and immunostaining data shown in Figure 1F and G.

claim: Atg9 null mutants displayed impaired developmental autophagy in the larval fat body.
source: Moreover, Atg9 null mutants displayed impaired developmental autophagy in the larval fat body and larval midgut (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Atg9 null mutants displayed impaired developmental autophagy in the larval midgut.
source: Moreover, Atg9 null mutants displayed impaired developmental autophagy in the larval fat body and larval midgut (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Atg9 is essential for autophagy during development and in response to starvation.
source: These results together demonstrate the essential role of Atg9 in autophagy during development and in response to starvation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple experimental observations in the manuscript.

claim: Many Drosophila autophagy mutants display reduced lifespan.
source: Many Drosophila autophagy mutants display reduced lifespan and decreased climbing activity (Juhász et al., 2007; Kim et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Many Drosophila autophagy mutants display decreased climbing activity.
source: Many Drosophila autophagy mutants display reduced lifespan and decreased climbing activity (Juhász et al., 2007; Kim et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The lifespan of Atg9 mutants was greatly reduced compared with that of Atg9 heterozygous control flies (48% decrease in male mean lifespan and 53% in female).
source: As shown in Figure 2A, we found that the lifespan of Atg9 mutants was greatly reduced compared with that of Atg9 heterozygous control flies (48% decrease in male mean lifespan and 53% in female, p<0.001) or Atg7 mutants (38% decrease in male mean lifespan and 40% in female, p<0.001) under normal conditions.
evidence: This is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The lifespan of Atg9 mutants was greatly reduced compared with that of Atg7 mutants (38% decrease in male mean lifespan and 40% in female).
source: As shown in Figure 2A, we found that the lifespan of Atg9 mutants was greatly reduced compared with that of Atg9 heterozygous control flies (48% decrease in male mean lifespan and 53% in female, p<0.001) or Atg7 mutants (38% decrease in male mean lifespan and 40% in female, p<0.001) under normal conditions.
evidence: This is supported by lifespan data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Atg9 mutants exhibited a significantly lowered climbing activity than that of the control flies.
source: The negative geotaxis assay also revealed that Atg9 mutants exhibited a significantly lowered climbing activity than that of the control flies (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by climbing assay data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The locomotion defects of Atg9 mutants were substantially suppressed by expressing the Atg9 genomic rescue construct.
source: The locomotion defects of Atg9 mutants were substantially suppressed by expressing the Atg9 genomic rescue construct, suggesting that the mobility defects were indeed caused by interruption of Atg9 gene expression.
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data.

claim: Loss of Atg9 leads to dramatically decreased viability under starvation conditions.
source: Moreover, loss of Atg9 leads to dramatically decreased viability under starvation and oxidative stress conditions (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by stress resistance data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Loss of Atg9 leads to dramatically decreased viability under oxidative stress conditions.
source: Moreover, loss of Atg9 leads to dramatically decreased viability under starvation and oxidative stress conditions (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This is supported by stress resistance data shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Atg9 regulates Drosophila lifespan, mobility, and susceptibility to stresses.
source: We thus conclude that, like other autophagy mutants, Atg9 also regulates Drosophila lifespan, mobility, and susceptibility to stresses.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on multiple experimental observations.

claim: The Drosophila adult midgut shares many similarities with the mammalian intestine.
source: The Drosophila adult midgut shares many similarities with the mammalian intestine and has emerged as an attractive model system to study stem cell proliferation and differentiation (Jiang and Edgar, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The Drosophila adult midgut has emerged as an attractive model system to study stem cell proliferation and differentiation.
source: The Drosophila adult midgut shares many similarities with the mammalian intestine and has emerged as an attractive model system to study stem cell proliferation and differentiation (Jiang and Edgar, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Drosophila Atg9 is involved in regulating adult midgut homeostasis upon ROS stimulation.
source: Our previous study showed that Drosophila Atg9 is involved in regulating adult midgut homeostasis upon ROS stimulation and bacterial infection (Tang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is from previous work by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: Drosophila Atg9 is involved in regulating adult midgut homeostasis upon bacterial infection.
source: Our previous study showed that Drosophila Atg9 is involved in regulating adult midgut homeostasis upon ROS stimulation and bacterial infection (Tang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is from previous work by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: The Drosophila adult midgut consists of a tubular, monolayered epithelium surrounded by visceral muscles.
source: The Drosophila adult midgut consists of a tubular, monolayered epithelium surrounded by visceral muscles (Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The Atg9 mutant adult midgut is markedly shortened compared to control flies.
source: In striking contrast, the Atg9 mutant adult midgut is markedly shortened and significantly thickened in the posterior region, compared to control flies (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The Atg9 mutant adult midgut is significantly thickened in the posterior region compared to control flies.
source: In striking contrast, the Atg9 mutant adult midgut is markedly shortened and significantly thickened in the posterior region, compared to control flies (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Loss of Atg9 leads to severe disruption in the continuity of the visceral mesoderm layer surrounding the gut.
source: Moreover, phalloidin staining of actin filaments in the visceral muscles revealed a severe disruption in the continuity of the visceral mesoderm layer surrounding the gut (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by phalloidin staining data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: There was a dramatic increase of Smurf+ flies in aged Atg9 mutant animals, compared to controls.
source: Although we found no significant intestinal barrier dysfunction in young Atg9 mutants, there was a dramatic increase of Smurf + flies in aged Atg9 mutant animals, compared to controls (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by Smurf assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The Drosophila adult midgut epithelium homeostasis is maintained by self-renewing intestinal stem cells (ISC) that divide asymmetrically.
source: The Drosophila adult midgut epithelium homeostasis is maintained by self-renewing intestinal stem cells (ISC) that divide asymmetrically to generate renewed ISCs and enteroblasts (EB) (Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006; Ohlstein and Spradling, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: ISCs divide asymmetrically to generate renewed ISCs and enteroblasts (EB).
source: The Drosophila adult midgut epithelium homeostasis is maintained by self-renewing intestinal stem cells (ISC) that divide asymmetrically to generate renewed ISCs and enteroblasts (EB) (Micchelli and Perrimon, 2006; Ohlstein and Spradling, 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The EB further differentiate into either absorptive enterocytes (EC) or secretory enteroendocrine cells (EE).
source: The EB further differentiate into either absorptive enterocytes (EC) or secretory enteroendocrine cells (EE).
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila midgut cell types.

claim: In Atg9 mutant flies, the epithelium is composed of dramatically enlarged cells.
source: In Atg9 mutant flies, the epithelium was also a monolayer, but composed of dramatically enlarged cells and abnormal apical membrane protrusions that often expanded into the midgut lumen (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This is supported by imaging and quantification data shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: In Atg9 mutant flies, the epithelium has abnormal apical membrane protrusions that often expanded into the midgut lumen.
source: In Atg9 mutant flies, the epithelium was also a monolayer, but composed of dramatically enlarged cells and abnormal apical membrane protrusions that often expanded into the midgut lumen (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This is supported by imaging data shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: The aberrant midgut defects in Atg9 mutants can be fully rescued by the Atg9 genomic transgene.
source: Notably, the aberrant midgut defects in Atg9 mutants can be fully rescued by the Atg9 genomic transgene (Figure 3C–E), further demonstrating that the intestinal defects were a direct consequence of the Atg9 mutation.
evidence: This is supported by rescue experiment data shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: There is no statistical difference in the number of PH3-positive cells between Atg9 null and control flies at both 5 days and 30 days of age.
source: Immunostaining with an antibody for the mitotic marker phospho-histone 3 (PH3) in the whole midgut revealed no statistical difference in the number of PH3-positive cells between Atg9 null and control flies at both 5 days and 30 days of age (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by PH3 staining and quantification data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The Atg9 mutant midgut showed a similar number of total intestinal cells compared with controls.
source: Moreover, the Atg9 mutant midgut showed a similar number of total intestinal cells, Delta-positive (ISC-specific marker) cells and Pros-positive (EE marker) cells, compared with controls (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The Atg9 mutant midgut showed a similar number of Delta-positive cells compared with controls.
source: Moreover, the Atg9 mutant midgut showed a similar number of total intestinal cells, Delta-positive (ISC-specific marker) cells and Pros-positive (EE marker) cells, compared with controls (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The Atg9 mutant midgut showed a similar number of Pros-positive cells compared with controls.
source: Moreover, the Atg9 mutant midgut showed a similar number of total intestinal cells, Delta-positive (ISC-specific marker) cells and Pros-positive (EE marker) cells, compared with controls (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by cell counting data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Atg9 is not required for the regulation of ISC proliferation under normal conditions.
source: Together, these results indicate that Atg9 is not required for the regulation of ISC proliferation under normal conditions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the proliferation and cell counting data.

claim: Atg9 depletion in ECs resulted in pronounced defects in the midgut epithelium, with a markedly increased cell size and aberrant cell morphology.
source: While Atg9 depletion in ISCs and EBs did not cause any observable defects in the midgut, Atg9 depletion in ECs resulted in pronounced defects in the midgut epithelium, with a markedly increased cell size and aberrant cell morphology (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by cell-type specific knockdown data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Atg9 depletion in ISCs did not cause any observable defects in the midgut.
source: While Atg9 depletion in ISCs and EBs did not cause any observable defects in the midgut, Atg9 depletion in ECs resulted in pronounced defects in the midgut epithelium, with a markedly increased cell size and aberrant cell morphology (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by cell-type specific knockdown data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Atg9 depletion in EBs did not cause any observable defects in the midgut.
source: While Atg9 depletion in ISCs and EBs did not cause any observable defects in the midgut, Atg9 depletion in ECs resulted in pronounced defects in the midgut epithelium, with a markedly increased cell size and aberrant cell morphology (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by cell-type specific knockdown data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The aberrant midgut enlargement is likely not caused by defects during development.
source: Because the midgut defects was only observed when Atg9RNAi was induced by temperature shift in adult flies with Tub-Gal4; Tub-Gal80ts as driver, the aberrant midgut enlargement is likely not caused by defects during development (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is based on temporal control experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Ablation of Atg9 with muscle-specific How-Gal4ts did not cause any observable defects in the adult midgut.
source: Moreover, although the visceral muscle defects were observed in Atg9 mutants (Figure 3B), we found that, like Atg9 depletion in ISCs and EBs, ablation of Atg9 with muscle-specific How-Gal4ts did not cause any observable defects in the adult midgut (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by muscle-specific knockdown data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mosaic analysis of Atg9 mutant clones revealed a dramatic increase in cell size of Atg9 mutant cells.
source: Mosaic analysis of Atg9 mutant clones revealed a dramatic increase in cell size of Atg9 mutant cells (Figure 4C, GFP-negative, encircled).
evidence: This is supported by clonal analysis data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Many of the enlarged GFP-positive cells in Atg9 mutant clone were stained positive for Pdm1.

claim: Atg9 acts largely in ECs to regulate cell growth.

claim: Activation of the Atg1 complex recruits and tethers Atg9-containing vesicles for the initiation of autophagy.

claim: Ablation of Atg9 suppresses Atg1-induced eye roughness in Drosophila.

claim: Ablation of Atg9 suppresses Atg1-induced wing vein defects in Drosophila.

claim: Overexpression of Atg1 can rescue the midgut defects caused by depletion of Atg9.

claim: Rapamycin treatment did not rescue the lifespan defects of Atg9 mutants.

claim: Overexpression of TSC1-TSC2 strongly suppressed Atg9RNAi-induced midgut defects.

evidence: This is supported by genetic interaction data shown in Figure 6D-H and L.

source: Overexpression of the TOR negative regulator TSC1-TSC2 (the tuberous sclerosis complex 1 and 2), the dominant-negative TOR (TORTED), the dominant-negative S6K (S6KKQ), or knockdown of TOR activator Rheb (RhebRNAi) strongly suppressed Atg9RNAi-induced midgut defects (Figure 6D–H,L).
evidence: This is supported by genetic interaction data shown in Figure 6D-H and L.

claim: Knockdown of TOR activator Rheb (RhebRNAi) strongly suppressed Atg9RNAi-induced midgut defects.
source: Overexpression of the TOR negative regulator TSC1-TSC2 (the tuberous sclerosis complex 1 and 2), the dominant-negative TOR (TORTED), the dominant-negative S6K (S6KKQ), or knockdown of TOR activator Rheb (RhebRNAi) strongly suppressed Atg9RNAi-induced midgut defects (Figure 6D–H,L).

claim: Patj forms a complex with the apical polarity protein Crumbs (Crb) and Stardust (Sdt; Pals1).

evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In mammals, Patj regulates tight junction formation and cell migration.

evidence: This is established knowledge from mammalian studies supported by citations.

claim: Depletion of Patj leads to increased TOR activity in human intestinal epithelial cells.
source: Interestingly, recent findings have shown that Patj can interact directly with TSC2 and depletion of Patj leads to increased TOR activity in human intestinal epithelial cells (Massey-Harroche et al., 2007; Rosner et al., 2008), suggesting that Patj may regulate TOR signaling through its interaction with TSC2.

claim: Patj can interact with TSC2 in Drosophila S2 cells.

claim: Depletion of Patj with NP1-Gal4 results in aberrant intestinal epithelium.

claim: Overexpression of Patj did not rescue the midgut defects caused by Atg1 depletion.
source: Overexpression of Patj in the midgut largely rescued the Atg9 depletion-induced midgut defects (60%, n = 24) but not the midgut defects caused by Atg1 or Atg17 depletion (Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B), whereas Patj depletion exacerbated the midgut defects caused by Atg9 ablation (Figure 7F).

evidence: This is supported by genetic interaction data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Patj depletion exacerbated the midgut defects caused by Atg9 ablation.
source: Overexpression of Patj in the midgut largely rescued the Atg9 depletion-induced midgut defects (60%, n = 24) but not the midgut defects caused by Atg1 or Atg17 depletion (Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and B), whereas Patj depletion exacerbated the midgut defects caused by Atg9 ablation (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by genetic interaction data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Ablation of Atg9 in EC cells leads to increased lethality in response to paraquat ingestion.

evidence: This is from previous work by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: Ectopic expression of Patj in EC cells significantly rescued the paraquat-induced lethality of Atg9 knockdown animals.

claim: TSC2 is a short-lived protein and is readily targeted for degradation.

claim: Depletion of Atg1 does not affect the association between Atg9, Patj and TSC2.
source: As shown in Figure 8A, Atg9 specifically interacted with TSC2 by immunoprecipitation experiments, and depletion of Atg1 does not affect the association between Atg9, Patj and TSC2 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Clonal depletion of Atg9 in the adult midgut caused a marked decrease in TSC2 levels.

claim: TSC2 levels were not affected in Atg1 knockdown cells.
source: More strikingly, clonal depletion of Atg9 (RFP-positive cells) in the adult midgut caused a marked decrease in TSC2 levels (Figure 8B), whereas TSC2 levels were not affected in Atg1 or Atg17 knockdown cells (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by clonal analysis data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

evidence: This is supported by clonal analysis data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Atg9 mutants exhibit severe defects in autophagy.
source: Similar to other autophagy mutants such as Atg7 and Atg17/Fip200 null flies (Juhász et al., 2007; Kim et al., 2013), Atg9 mutants exhibit severe defects in autophagy, shortened lifespan, impaired motility, and hypersensitivity to stresses.

claim: Atg9 loss-of-function leads to aberrant midgut enlargement.

claim: Atg9 loss-of-function leads to intestinal barrier dysfunction.
source: Atg9 loss-of-function also leads to aberrant midgut enlargement and intestinal barrier dysfunction.
evidence: This is a summary of findings from the manuscript.

claim: Depletion of Atg7 in adult flies did not cause aberrant midgut enlargement.

claim: Depletion of Atg7 in adult flies did not cause intestinal barrier dysfunction.
source: Interestingly, we found that, unlike Atg9 mutant, depletion of Atg7 in adult flies did not cause aberrant midgut enlargement or intestinal barrier dysfunction (Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).

claim: The adult midgut defects may contribute to the much shorter lifespan of Atg9 mutants.

claim: Atg9 not only acts as a key regulator in autophagy but also functions in maintaining adult Drosophila midgut homeostasis.
source: Our findings indicate that Atg9 not only acts as a key regulator in autophagy but also functions in maintaining adult Drosophila midgut homeostasis.

claim: The Drosophila adult midgut is composed of a monolayer of epithelial cells including nutrient absorbing enterocytes (ECs), secretory enteroendocrine (EE) cells, and multipotent intestinal stem cells (ISCs).
source: The Drosophila adult midgut is composed of a monolayer of epithelial cells including nutrient absorbing enterocytes (ECs), secretory enteroendocrine (EE) cells, and multipotent intestinal stem cells (ISCs) (Lemaitre and Miguel-Aliaga, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: A number of conserved signaling pathways have been shown to be involved in the regulation of ISC proliferation and in the maintenance of tissue homeostasis of the Drosophila midgut.

evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: ISCs are the only dividing cells in the Drosophila adult midgut.
source: ISCs are the only dividing cells in the Drosophila adult midgut and play an essential role in maintaining tissue homeostasis.

claim: ISCs play an essential role in maintaining tissue homeostasis in the Drosophila adult midgut.
source: ISCs are the only dividing cells in the Drosophila adult midgut and play an essential role in maintaining tissue homeostasis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about Drosophila midgut biology.

claim: Loss of Atg9 does not affect ISC proliferation.
source: However, we found that the total number of intestinal cells and Delta+ ISC population were not affected in Atg9 mutants. PH3 staining of control or Atg9 mutant midguts at young (5 day) or old (30 day) stages showed similar numbers of mitotic ISCs in both animals, thus indicating that loss of Atg9 does not affect ISC proliferation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on cell counting and PH3 staining data.

claim: Insulin and TOR signaling are conserved nutrient-sensing pathways involved in regulating cell growth, metabolism and tissue homeostasis.
source: Insulin and TOR signaling are conserved nutrient-sensing pathways involved in regulating cell growth, metabolism and tissue homeostasis (Oldham and Hafen, 2003).

claim: Insulin and TOR signaling regulate enterocyte growth and endoreduplication in the adult Drosophila midgut.

evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Atg9 may act as a negative regulator of TOR-mediated cell growth.

evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental observations.

claim: Atg9 depletion did not cause an increase in larval disc cell size.

claim: Normal development and tissue homeostasis is maintained by a delicate coordination between cell growth and division.

evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: ECs in adult midgut are non-dividing differentiated cells.
source: One possible explanation for this difference is that ECs in adult midgut are non-dividing differentiated cells, whereas larval disc cells are active dividing cells and therefore maintain a moderate cell size.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cell types.

claim: Larval disc cells are active dividing cells.
source: One possible explanation for this difference is that ECs in adult midgut are non-dividing differentiated cells, whereas larval disc cells are active dividing cells and therefore maintain a moderate cell size.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cell types.

claim: Overexpression of Atg1 rescued Atg9RNAi-induced midgut defects.

claim: Overexpression of Atg9 could not suppress the midgut defects caused by Atg1 depletion.

claim: Atg9 can still interact with Patj and TSC2 in Atg1 knockdown S2 cells.

claim: Atg1 inhibits TOR signaling independent of Atg9.

claim: In mammals, Atg1/Ulk1 inhibits TOR signaling by phosphorylating Raptor and impairs substrate binding to Raptor.
source: In mammals, it has been shown that Atg1/Ulk1 inhibits TOR signaling by phosphorylating Raptor and impairs substrate binding to Raptor (Dunlop et al., 2011; Jung et al., 2011), and the inhibitory effect of Ulk1 on TOR signaling occurred independently of TSC2 (Jung et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge from mammalian studies supported by citations.

claim: The inhibitory effect of Ulk1 on TOR signaling occurred independently of TSC2.
source: In mammals, it has been shown that Atg1/Ulk1 inhibits TOR signaling by phosphorylating Raptor and impairs substrate binding to Raptor (Dunlop et al., 2011; Jung et al., 2011), and the inhibitory effect of Ulk1 on TOR signaling occurred independently of TSC2 (Jung et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge from mammalian studies supported by citation.

source: The Drosophila epithelial polarity is regulated by evolutionarily conserved polarity protein complexes including the Crumbs (Crb)/Stardust (Sdt)/Patj complex, the Bazooka (Baz)/Par6/aPKC complex and the Scribble/Discs large (Dlg)/Lethal giant larva (Lgl) complex (Tepass, 2012).

source: The scaffolding protein Patj interacts with both Crb-Std and Baz-Std apical polarity protein complexes, and has been shown to play a non-essential role in apical-basal polarity during Drosophila development (Pénalva and Mirouse, 2012; Sen et al., 2015; Zhou and Hong, 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Patj has been shown to cycle between plasma membrane and endosomal compartments in mammalian cells.
source: Interestingly, like Atg9, Patj has been shown to cycle between plasma membrane and endosomal compartments in mammalian cells (Heller et al., 2010; Wells et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established knowledge from mammalian studies supported by citations.
